'''''Urochloa mutica''''', commonly known as '''para grass''', '''buffalo grass''', '''Mauritius signal grass''', '''pasto pare''', '''malojilla''', '''gramalote''', '''parana''', '''Carib grass''', and '''Scotch grass''', is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]].<ref name=feis>Stone, Katharine R. 2010. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/graminoid/uromut/all.html ''Urochloa mutica''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory.</ref><ref name=smith>[http://www.sms.si.edu/irlspec/urochloa_mutica.htm ''Urochloa mutica''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009173507/http://www.sms.si.edu/irlspec/Urochloa_mutica.htm |date=2016-10-09 }} Smithsonian Marine Station at Fort Pierce.</ref> Despite its common name of '''California grass''',<ref name=feis/> it does not occur in [[California]];<ref name=usda>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=URMU ''Urochloa mutica''.] USDA Plants Profile.</ref> it is native to northern and central Africa and parts of the Middle East, where it is cultivated for [[fodder]].<ref name=smith/> It was [[introduced species|introduced]] elsewhere and it is now cultivated throughout tropical regions of the world for this purpose.<ref name=feis/>

==Description==
Para grass is a vigorous, semi-prostrate perennial grass with creeping stolons which can grow up to {{convert|5|m|ft|0}} long. The stems have hairy nodes and leaf sheaths and the leaf blades are up to {{convert|2|cm|in|1}} wide and {{convert|30|cm|in|0}} long. It roots at the nodes and detached pieces of the plant will easily take root in moist ground. The flower-head is a loose [[panicle]] up to {{convert|30|cm|in|0}} long with spreading branches. The paired [[Poaceae#Description|spikelets]] are arranged in uneven rows and are elliptical and {{convert|2.5|to|5|mm|in|1}} long. The [[rachis]] is tinged with purple. Although many flower-heads grow, only a few viable seeds are produced, and propagation is usually by vegetative means.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /><ref name=smith/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tropicalforages.info/key/Forages/Media/Html/Brachiaria_mutica.htm |title=''Brachiaria mutica'' |publisher=Tropical Forages |access-date=2015-07-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150717022337/http://www.tropicalforages.info/key/Forages/Media/Html/Brachiaria_mutica.htm |archive-date=2015-07-17 }}</ref><ref name=usda1>[http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/para-grass.pdf ''Urochloa mutica''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305072150/http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/para-grass.pdf |date=2016-03-05 }} USDA Forest Service Weed of the Week.</ref> Para grass can be distinguished from the closely related tanner grass (''[[Brachiaria arrecta]]'') by its paired spikelets, tanner grass having single spikelets.<ref name=Miles/>

==Distribution and habitat==
Para grass is native to northern and central Africa and parts of the Middle East.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> It was introduced into Central America but has largely been superseded there by other species of ''[[Brachiaria]]''. It was also introduced into the humid, tropical parts of Australia around 1880 and has become widely naturalised in [[Queensland]]. By a few decades later it had become naturalised in much of southern Asia and on many Pacific islands, but is confined to its preferred habitat of poorly drained, swampy land. Along with tanner grass, it is planted as a fodder grass in seasonally flooded or swampy habitats, and in ponds in pastures, but it can block irrigation ditches and drains.<ref name=Miles>{{cite book|author1=Miles, John W.|author2=Maass, Brigitte L.|author3=Cacilda Borges Valle|title=Brachiaria: Biology, Agronomy, and Improvement|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dMF6QpfVdjMC&pg=PA20 |year=1996 |publisher=CIAT |isbn=978-958-9439-57-9 |pages=20, 259}}</ref> When used as forage for cattle it is usually controlled by the action of the animals, so it does not become too weedy. When it grows in other habitats, however, it can become [[noxious weed|noxious]]. It is aggressive and can form dense stands. It may also have [[allelopathy|allelopathic]] effects on other plants, preventing their growth.<ref name=fla>[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/71 ''Urochloa mutica''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721193114/http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/71 |date=2015-07-21 }} Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants, University of Florida.</ref>

This species may have been introduced to the Americas on [[slave ship]]s, on which it was used for bedding. It was in South America by the early 1800s and Mexico by 1872. It was introduced to [[Florida]] by the late 1870s to be used as fodder. It has since [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] in many areas and it now grows as a widespread weed. It is sensitive to [[frost]] so it generally does not persist outside warm regions.<ref name=feis/>

==Uses==
Para grass is mainly cultivated to feed livestock as it makes a high quality forage for ruminant animals.<ref>Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., Sauvant D., Lebas F., 2018. Para grass (Brachiaria mutica). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/486</ref>

==Invasive species==
The plant is an [[invasive species]] in many [[Pacific Island]]s and [[Pacific Rim]] countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution.asp?si=1600&fr=1&sts=sss&lang=EN|title=Global Invasive Species Database: Distribution of Urochloa mutica|publisher=Invasive Species Specialist Group|access-date=25 August 2012|archive-date=21 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721123829/http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution.asp?si=1600&fr=1&sts=sss&lang=EN|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Australia===
The species has invaded the northern and north-western areas of Australia has the potential to spread further inland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=nt&s=&region=gup&card=G08|title=Weed Identification - Para Grass|publisher=Weeds Australia|access-date=25 August 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110402103332/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=nt&s=&region=gup&card=G08|archive-date=2 April 2011}}</ref> It is present in [[Kakadu National Park]]. In Australia, this grass forms vast stands, destroying [[waterfowl]] nesting habitat and displacing native plants.<ref name=au>[http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=G08 ''Urochloa mutica''.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150331092037/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=G08 |date=March 31, 2015 }} National Weeds Strategy.</ref><ref name=flora>[http://florabase.dec.wa.gov.au/browse/profile/716 ''Urochloa mutica''.] FloraBase: The Western Australian Flora.</ref>

===United States===
In Florida this grass grows in various wetland habitat types, such as [[marsh]]es and [[floodplain]]s, as well as disturbed areas such as roadsides. In [[Hawaii]] this grass is widespread, especially in freshwater wetlands and in [[Rhizophora mangle|red mangrove]] (''Rhizophora mangle'') stands. It is thought to be a cause of the decline of the rare Hawaiian [[endemism|endemic]] [[Thelypteris boydiae|Boyd's maiden fern]] (''Thelypteris boydiae'').<ref name=feis/>
